document.title: The King James Version of the Bible

quotes.quote: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.

differs: In the King James Version, Genesis tells that God "created man in his own image", that "the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life", and that he made the woman from a rib taken from Adam in "a deep sleep"; it says nothing of genes or of any earlier humans altered, so the reading as a genetic manipulation is the teller's own.

document.title: The King James Version of the Bible

quotes.quote: And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not.
And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD.

And the LORD said unto Moses, Speak unto Aaron thy brother, that he come not at all times into the holy place within the vail before the mercy seat, which is upon the ark; that he die not: for I will appear in the cloud upon the mercy seat.

differs: The teller names the Book of Exodus but not a passage, and no verse in the books of Moses says that fire comes out of the Ark. If he means the deaths of Aaron's sons, then the source says "there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them" (Leviticus 10:2), and it warns Aaron to keep from "the mercy seat, which is upon the ark; that he die not" (Leviticus 16:2). The deaths at the Ark itself are told in the books of Samuel, which name no author: Uzzah, who "died by the ark of God" when God "smote him" (2 Samuel 6:7), and the men of Bethshemesh smitten "because they had looked into the ark of the LORD" (1 Samuel 6:19); neither passage speaks of fire.

document.title: The King James Version of the Bible

quotes.quote: For they are the spirits of devils, working miracles, which go forth unto the kings of the earth and of the whole world, to gather them to the battle of that great day of God Almighty.
And he gathered them together into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon.
And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war.
And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies, gathered together to make war against him that sat on the horse, and against his army.
And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which sword proceeded out of his mouth: and all the fowls were filled with their flesh.

differs: In the Revelation, Armageddon is the place where the kings of the earth are gathered "to the battle of that great day of God Almighty" (16:14, 16:16); the war against the rider on the white horse, called "The Word of God", is told in chapter 19, where the remnant are slain "with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which sword proceeded out of his mouth" (19:21). The text does not call the rider the Son of God in that chapter, and whether the war is a physical one is the teller's reading.

quotes.quote: And in the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel;
Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz:

His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.

differs: The King James Version names the river Hiddekel (Daniel 10:4), the Hebrew name of the Tigris; the being is described as "a certain man clothed in linen" whose face was "as the appearance of lightning" and who says "Fear not, Daniel" before telling what will befall Daniel's people.

quotes.quote: And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom: and Lot seeing them rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground;
For we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the LORD; and the LORD hath sent us to destroy it.
And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot, saying, Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters, which are here; lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city.

And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.
Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;

quotes.quote: And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them,
That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.

There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.

differs: Genesis 6 tells of "the sons of God" who took wives of "the daughters of men" and of "giants in the earth in those days"; it does not call them Watchers or angels, give their number, or name Mount Hermon, which are the Book of Enoch's.

document.title: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)

quotes.quote: Throw down the house, build a ship,
Carry grain of every kind into the ship.
The cattle of the field, the beasts of the field, all handicraftsmen I made them go up into it.
The storm raged, and the cyclone overwhelmed the land.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.
I brought out a dove and let her go free.
I brought out a swallow and let her go free.
I brought out a raven and let her go free.
She ate, she pecked in the ground, she croaked, she came not back.

differs: The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood. The comparison with Genesis is the teller's: the epic names neither Noah nor Genesis.

document.title: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)

quotes.quote: Their hearts induced the great gods to make a wind-storm
The Power of Darkness made a rain-flood to fall at eventide.
A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up.
Inside it the god Adad (Rammânu) thundered,
The Anunnaki [13] brandished their torches,
With their glare they lighted up the land.
The whirlwind (or, cyclone) of Adad swept up to heaven.

differs: The teller does not say which part of the epic he means; if it is the flood of the Eleventh Tablet, then the source says the great gods resolved "to make a wind-storm", and tells a rain-flood, "a black cloud from the foundation of heaven" in which Adad thundered, and the Anunnaki, whom the translator glosses as "the star-gods of the southern sky", brandishing their torches; it tells of nothing striking the earth. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.

document.title: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)

quotes.quote: O man of Shurippak, son of Ubara-Tutu.
The ship took its course to the land of Nisir.
The mountain of Nisir held the ship, it let it not move.

differs: The epic gives Uta-Napishtim as the "man of Shurippak" and has the ship held by "the mountain of Nisir"; it does not name Ararat, which is the Bible's "mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4), or the name Ziusudra. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.
